title.en: Speculative Decoding: The Accept/Reject Rule That Skips the Wait

description.en: A small draft model guesses tokens ahead; the big target model checks them all in one pass. The accept/reject rule decides which guesses survive — without ever changing what the model would have said anyway.

story_variants.en:
## Why Wait For One Token At A Time?

"Every token an LLM generates costs one full forward pass through a giant network," Vaathiyaar says. "That's true whether the token is 'the' or 'defenestration' — the model can't skip work just because a word is easy. **Speculative decoding** cheats around this: let a small, fast **draft model** guess a handful of tokens ahead, then have the big **target model** check all of them in a single forward pass."

### Checking Isn't Just Rubber-Stamping

The target model can't simply accept whatever the draft proposed — that would make the draft model's weaknesses the final output. Instead it uses a mathematically exact **accept/reject rule** (from 'Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding', 2023): for a token the draft proposed with probability `p_draft`, and the target model's own probability for that same token `p_target`:

```
accept_prob = min(1, p_target / p_draft)
accept if u < accept_prob        # u is a fresh Uniform(0, 1) draw
```

- If the target agrees at least as strongly as the draft did (`p_target >= p_draft`), `accept_prob` is capped at 1: **always accept**, pure free speed.
- If the target is less confident than the draft was, `accept_prob` shrinks proportionally: a **probabilistic** accept.
- On reject, the draft's guess is discarded and the target contributes its own token instead — so the *distribution* of final text is provably identical to running the target model alone, token by token, every single time.

### A Real Roll

Say the draft model was fairly confident about a word (`p_draft = 0.6`), but the target model only gives that same word `p_target = 0.3`. Then `accept_prob = min(1, 0.3 / 0.6) = 0.5` — a coin flip. Draw `u = 0.42`: since `0.42 < 0.5`, this particular guess is **accepted**, even though the target was less sure than the draft. Half the time, the same setup would reject instead — and that's exactly the point: the math guarantees the *long-run* output distribution never drifts from the target model's own.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** speculative decoding never changes WHAT the model says, only HOW FAST it says it. That losslessness is why every major inference stack — vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and friends — ships it as free speed, not a quality tradeoff.

Today you implement `speculative_accept(p_draft, p_target, u)` — the single-token core of the whole technique.

uth_example:
import random

draft_tokens = [                         # (token, p_draft, p_target)
    ("The", 0.60, 0.70),
    ("quick", 0.50, 0.45),
    ("purple", 0.40, 0.05),              # the small model guessed badly
    ("fox", 0.30, 0.60),
]
rng = random.Random(3)                   # fixed seed, so the run is repeatable

accepted = []
for token, p_draft, p_target in draft_tokens:
    accept_prob = min(1.0, p_target / p_draft)
    u = round(rng.random(), 3)
    if u < accept_prob:
        accepted.append(token)
    else:
        accepted.append("<resample>")    # the target model picks this token instead
        break                            # later drafts are thrown away
print("kept:", accepted)

under_the_hood.summary: A draft model proposes a token with probability p_draft; the target model accepts it with probability min(1, p_target / p_draft) or else resamples from the leftover distribution, so the output follows exactly the target model's distribution.

steps.title: Why the big model is slow
steps.body: Each generated token needs one full forward pass of the large model, and that pass is mostly limited by reading its weights from memory. Checking several tokens in one pass costs about the same as generating one.

steps.title: Draft, then verify in parallel
steps.body: The draft model proposes a few tokens quickly. The target model then runs once over the prompt plus all drafted tokens and gets its probability for each drafted token at each position.

steps.title: The acceptance rule
steps.body: accept_prob = min(1, p_target / p_draft). If the target likes the token at least as much as the draft did, it is always accepted. With p_draft = 0.6 and p_target = 0.3, accept_prob = 0.5; a uniform random u = 0.42 is below 0.5, so it is accepted.

steps.title: On rejection, resample the leftover
steps.body: If rejected, the token is replaced by a sample from max(0, p_target - p_draft), renormalised over the vocabulary. That puts back exactly the probability the draft under-weighted.

steps.title: Why the output is unchanged
steps.body: Accepting with probability min(1, p_t / p_d) and otherwise sampling the leftover makes the final token distribution exactly p_target. Speculative decoding is therefore a pure speed-up: same distribution, fewer slow passes.

under_the_hood.takeaway: The accept/reject rule lets a cheap model do most of the guessing while the expensive model keeps full control of the output distribution.
